## State Preservation

Machine suspend lets you pause a running Fly Machine and save its complete state, including memory, to persistent storage. Suspend automatically saves a machine's memory state to persistent storage. You don't need to attach a volume for suspend to work, and the snapshot isn't stored on a volume.

## Resume Speed

Starting a Machine from a suspended state is faster than starting a Machine from a stopped state. Additionally, Machines in suspended preserve memory and disk state, and resume faster than stopped.

## Resume Process

Suspended Machines that are started attempt to resume from the snapshot taken when they were suspended. If this is not possible, then they will perform a cold boot, as though starting from the stopped state; however, their root file systems will not be reset.

## Important Caveats

Snapshots are tied to the exact code and state of the machine they were taken from. If you deploy new code, the old snapshot can't be resumed safely and will be discarded.

## Scale to Zero with State Preservation

It'll take your application, save its state, and then reduce its running instances to zero. What doesn't go away are the networking configuration, IP addresses and certificates, which are maintained in the background.

## Durable Objects as the Actor Model Foundation

The agent is a Durable Object — a single, addressable, stateful micro-server with its own embedded SQLite database, its own WebSocket connections, and its own scheduler. Durable Objects are described through the lens of the Actor programming model, which simplifies distributed systems problems by abstracting away communication between actors using RPC calls and avoiding concurrency pitfalls from shared memory.

## Per-User AI Agent Architecture

Instead of "one expensive agent per power user," you can build "one agent per customer" or "one agent per task" or "one agent per email thread," with the marginal cost of spawning a new agent being effectively zero. For human-in-the-loop use cases, you have an agent process, and therefore a durable object, per-user.

## Scale-to-Zero Capabilities

Each instance has persistent state that survives restarts, deploys, and failures; each instance is a single-writer actor, so its state can't be corrupted by concurrent requests; and each instance costs nothing while it's idle. Agents consume zero compute when hibernated, and when something happens (an HTTP request, a WebSocket message, a scheduled alarm, an inbound email) the platform wakes the agent, loads its state, and hands it the event.

Agents hibernate when idle and wake on demand, and you can run millions of them — one per user, per session, per game room — each costs nothing when inactive.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Modal sandbox memory snapshot restore and cold start:

## Overview

Modal Memory Snapshots can dramatically reduce the cold start latency of Modal Functions by skipping initialization work on most container boots.

## How It Works

Sandbox memory snapshots are copies of a Sandbox's entire state, both in memory and on the filesystem. These Snapshots can be restored later to create a new Sandbox, which is an exact clone of the original Sandbox.

A Modal memory snapshot is a couple of files that represent the entire state of a Linux container right before it was about to accept a request. The snapshot captures the container's filesystem mutations and its entire process tree. Each process in that tree has state consisting of its memory mappings, file descriptor table, registers, environment variables, process ID, and more.

## Performance Benefits

Memory snapshot restore is about 2.5x faster than a standard container startup. A Stable Diffusion inference Function that takes around 13 seconds normally restores in only 3.5 seconds. In practical experience, initialization-heavy Functions often start up 3-10x faster from Memory Snapshots.

## Recent Developments (2025)

Memory snapshots were introduced in January 2025. More recently, GPU memory snapshots were introduced to bring checkpoint/restore functionality to GPU-accelerated workloads. Functions have been observed starting up to 10x times faster than baseline with GPU memory snapshots.

## Limitations

Memory Snapshots expire 7 days after creation and cannot currently be extended. Sandbox memory snapshots can only be restored on the same exact instance type that the original Sandbox was run on. Given Modal's diverse fleet of capacity, this can sometimes lead to scheduling delays, especially when memory snapshots are combined with narrow region pinning.

## Letta Server Architecture

Letta is a stateful agent server with a proper REST API, a TypeScript/Node.js client, PostgreSQL-backed persistence, and a web-based Agent Development Environment (ADE). The key architectural commitment Letta makes is that the server owns all state—when you send a new user message, the Letta server handles the rest: it injects the right memory blocks, runs the agent, manages the context window, persists everything to its internal PostgreSQL database, and returns the response.

## Agents as Data with Database Persistence

In Letta, all state, including memories, user messages, reasoning, and tool calls, are all persisted in a database, so they are never lost, even once evicted from the context window. Important "core" memories are injected into the context window of the LLM, and the agent can modify its own memories through tools.

## Sleep-Time Agents Architecture

In Letta, you can create special sleep-time agents that share the memory of your primary agents, but run in the background and can modify the memory asynchronously. A single agent can have one or more associated sleep-time agents to process data such as the conversation history or data sources to manage the memory blocks of the primary agent.

## Webhook vs Long Polling Overview

Telegram Bot API provides two ways for your bot to receive updates: long polling and webhook. Each approach has distinct trade-offs for development, performance, and scalability.

With long polling, your bot continuously calls the getUpdates method in a loop. Telegram holds the connection open until new updates are available (or a timeout is reached), then responds with them.

With webhook, you register an HTTPS URL with Telegram. When an update arrives, Telegram sends an HTTP POST request to that URL with the update payload.

## Scaling Considerations

Telegram rejects concurrent getUpdates calls from the same bot token. If two processes poll at the same time, one gets a 409 Conflict error.

For webhook scaling: When scaling with webhook, ensure your bot logic is stateless (or uses shared storage like Redis for sessions). Each update may arrive at a different pod.

## Update_id Deduplication and Idempotency

Telegram may retry an update if your HTTP response is missing or code ≥500. De-duplicate using update_id.

Always implement idempotency using update_id; replays can occur during retries.

Store update_id in a 1 h TTL cache to de-duplicate during your own fail-over.

Telegram does not guarantee ordered delivery under retry storms; your handler must be idempotent.

## When to Use Each Approach

If daily messages >10 k or latency SLA <2 s → choose webhooks. The main advantage of webhooks over long polling is that they are cheaper. You save a ton of superfluous requests.

### Single Bot with Per-User/Per-Topic Routing
One process can handle multiple agents through a shared daemon with one Telegram bot token and one Discord bot connection, while memory isolation ensures Agent A's memory is never visible to Agent B, and agents are logical tenants inside the daemon, not separate processes. ## Multi-Tenant Data Isolation

Multi-tenancy can be implemented through AsyncLocalStorage, a Node.js mechanism for storing context within the scope of a single request. # Machine Suspend and Resume: Summary

## Speed
Resume from suspend is dramatically faster than cold starts: "a few hundred ms" versus "~2+ seconds for common apps."

## Memory & Hardware Limits
Machines must have:
- **≤ 2 GB memory** (larger sizes discouraged due to increased suspend times)
- No swap configured
- No GPU configured
- No schedule configured
- Updated since June 20, 2024

## Volume Behavior
Volumes are unaffected by suspend/resume. Data persists across suspension cycles. The snapshot and volume are managed separately—deployments discard snapshots but preserve volume data.

## Key Caveats
- Snapshots aren't guaranteed to persist; new deployments discard old snapshots
- "Some logs may be lost after resume"
- Network connections may stale; applications should implement reconnection logic
- Clock can lag a few seconds until NTP syncs
- Unlike `stop`, suspend doesn't reset the machine's root filesystem

## Stop vs. Suspend
Stop is a full shutdown; suspend preserves memory state. Suspend enables much faster recovery but requires careful network connection handling post-resume.

## Billing
Suspended machines cost the same as stopped machines (storage only, no CPU/RAM charges). Suspension reserves regional capacity and doesn't free it up.

# Multi-Tenant Agent Hosting: 2025–2026 Best Practices Research Report

Scope: a free pilot where each signup provisions a persistent, personal AI agent (currently: one always-on Docker container per user on a single VM), reached via a dedicated Telegram bot. Findings below are organized per your six questions, with sources per claim and explicit uncertainty notes.

---

## 1. Scale-to-zero patterns for per-user workloads

**The consensus 2025–2026 pattern:** don't keep per-user processes running; keep per-user *state* durable and cheap, and attach compute only when a message arrives. Every major platform has converged on some form of this.

### Activation-on-message (queue in front, container started on demand)
- The self-hosted version of this is exactly what **Sablier** implements: a reverse-proxy middleware (Traefik/Nginx/Caddy) that starts a Docker container on the first incoming request and stops it after inactivity. It also has a "scale mode" that throttles CPU/memory instead of stopping, avoiding cold starts entirely. Works with plain Docker, Swarm, Podman, K8s, Proxmox LXC. ([github.com/sablierapp/sablier](https://github.com/sablierapp/sablier), [sablierapp.dev](https://sablierapp.dev/), [production-ready.de writeup](https://www.production-ready.de/2023/08/20/docker-scale-to-zero-with-traefik-sablier-en.html))
- On Kubernetes, **KEDA** scales deployments to zero and wakes them on queue depth or HTTP events (HTTP add-on still beta). ([Google Cloud blog](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/containers-kubernetes/scale-to-zero-on-gke-with-keda/), [GKE tutorial](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/tutorials/scale-to-zero-using-keda))
- For your Telegram shape specifically, the queue-in-front pattern is natural: a single always-on lightweight gateway receives all webhook updates, enqueues them per-user, and a supervisor `docker start`s (or unpauses) the user's container, delivers the queued messages, and stops it after N minutes idle. Sablier is HTTP-oriented, so for message-driven wake you'd likely write a small supervisor yourself (this is a modest amount of code: Docker API `start`/`stop` + a per-user queue with a debounce window).

### Fly.io Machines: suspend/resume — fast, and state is preserved
- Suspend saves the Machine's **full memory state** to persistent storage (no volume needed). Resume is "**a few hundred ms**" vs ~2+ seconds for a cold start of a typical app. ([fly.io/docs/reference/suspend-resume](https://fly.io/docs/reference/suspend-resume/))
- Hard limits that matter for you: suspendable Machines must have **≤ 2 GB RAM**, no swap, no GPU. Snapshots are discarded on redeploy (new code ⇒ cold boot, rootfs preserved). Network connections go stale across resume — your agent runtime must reconnect; clock lags a few seconds until NTP resync. ([same doc](https://fly.io/docs/reference/suspend-resume/))
- Fly also has plain autostop/autostart (stop on idle, start on request via their proxy) and "Power Pause". ([fly.io/docs/launch/autostop-autostart](https://fly.io/docs/launch/autostop-autostart/), [Power Pause blog](https://fly.io/blog/fly-now-with-power-pause/))
- Economics: **stopped/suspended Machines cost only rootfs storage — $0.15/GB/month**. So 1,000 idle per-user agents with 1 GB rootfs ≈ $150/mo idle cost plus compute only while awake. This is arguably the closest managed analog to your current architecture (one persistent container per user) with scale-to-zero bolted on. ([fly.io/docs/about/pricing](https://fly.io/docs/about/pricing/), [community announcement of rootfs charges](https://community.fly.io/t/we-are-going-to-start-collecting-charges-for-stopped-machines-rootfs-starting-april-25th/17825))

### Cloudflare Durable Objects / Agents SDK
- A Cloudflare Agent literally *is* a Durable Object: one addressable, single-threaded actor per user with its own embedded SQLite, WebSockets, and alarms/scheduler. It hibernates when idle (**zero compute cost while inactive**), and the platform wakes it on HTTP request, WebSocket message, alarm, or email. Marginal cost of "one agent per user" is ~zero; millions of instances are the intended usage. ([developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/concepts/what-are-durable-objects/), [blog.cloudflare.com/project-think](https://blog.cloudflare.com/project-think/), [agents.cloudflare.com](https://agents.cloudflare.com/), [truvisory analysis](https://truvisory.com/agents-mcp/agents-sdk-durable-objects/))
- Constraint: DOs run JS/WASM in isolates — you can't run an arbitrary Node.js Docker image inside one. **Cloudflare Containers** (public beta since June 2025) closes that gap: each unique ID gets a container instance routed via a DO, which boots on first fetch and sleeps after a configurable `sleepAfter` timeout; billing stops while asleep (memory $0.0000025/GiB-s; requires $5/mo Workers Paid). Note: sleeping a Cloudflare Container loses memory state (it's stop/start, not suspend) — persistent state must live in the DO's SQLite or external storage. ([blog.cloudflare.com containers beta](https://blog.cloudflare.com/containers-are-available-in-public-beta-for-simple-global-and-programmable/), [containers pricing](https://developers.cloudflare.com/containers/pricing/), [devclass coverage](https://devclass.com/2025/07/01/cloudflare-container-platform-in-public-preview-with-scale-to-zero-pricing-some-initial-limitations/))

### Modal
- Modal Sandboxes support **memory snapshots**: full state (filesystem + entire process tree memory) checkpointed and restored as an exact clone. Restores are ~2.5x faster than cold container start; init-heavy workloads see 3–10x. Introduced Jan 2025. Caveats: snapshots **expire after 7 days**, and restore requires the same instance type, which can cause scheduling delays. ([modal.com/docs/guide/memory-snapshots](https://modal.com/docs/guide/memory-snapshots), [sandbox snapshots](https://modal.com/docs/guide/sandbox-snapshots), [blog](https://modal.com/blog/mem-snapshots)) The 7-day expiry makes "resume a user's agent after 3 idle weeks" awkward unless you treat snapshots as a warm-start optimization over durable state, not the source of truth.

### AWS Fargate / Lambda for this shape
- **Fargate does not scale to zero** — a bot-per-user fleet of Fargate tasks reproduces your exact cost problem ($48–95/month-region per always-on minimum task). **Lambda scales to zero and bills per invocation**, but it's stateless with a 15-minute max execution — fine for "wake, load state, respond, exit" agents, poor for long agentic runs or in-memory continuity. Break-even analyses put Lambda ahead for spiky/infrequent traffic (your idle-most-of-the-time profile) and Fargate ahead for sustained load. ([AWS decision guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/decision-guides/latest/fargate-or-lambda/fargate-or-lambda.html), [CloudZero](https://www.cloudzero.com/blog/fargate-vs-lambda/), [LeanOps break-even analysis](https://leanopstech.com/blog/aws-lambda-vs-fargate-cost-breakeven-2026/)) AWS's own answer for persistent agents is Bedrock AgentCore-style managed runtimes rather than raw Fargate ([Medium overview](https://medium.com/@loic.labeye/lambda-fargate-agentcore-which-severless-option-to-choose-for-your-agentic-pattern-aaf68cb99700)) — uncertainty flag: I did not deep-verify AgentCore specifics in this pass.

**Bottom line for #1:** cheapest-to-adopt for your current design is (a) self-hosted wake-on-message (Sablier-style supervisor + queue) on your existing VM, or (b) lift the per-user container to Fly Machines with autostop/suspend (~$0.15/GB/mo idle, sub-second-ish resume). The deeper rearchitecture is the actor model (next section).

---

## 2. The actor model: state-as-data + shared worker pool

This is the pattern with the strongest 2025–2026 momentum, and it directly attacks your bottleneck: **the agent is a row/file, not a process.**

- **Letta** (ex-MemGPT) is the canonical "agents as data" precedent: a single stateful server owns all agent state in PostgreSQL — memory blocks, message history, tool state. Agents don't run as processes; the server hydrates an agent's context on each interaction, runs the LLM loop, persists, and returns. Thousands of "agents" are just DB rows; compute is a shared pool. ([docs.letta.com/core-concepts](https://docs.letta.com/core-concepts/), [stateful agents overview](https://docs.letta.com/guides/agents/overview/), [architecture writeup](https://sudoall.com/letta-stateful-agents-nodejs/))
- **Cloudflare Durable Objects** — virtual-actor semantics: single-writer per actor (no concurrent-write corruption), state survives restarts/deploys, zero idle cost, wake-on-event. ([developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/concepts/what-are-durable-objects/))
- **Rivet Actors** — explicitly markets "one actor per agent/session/user": long-lived lightweight processes, in-memory state with automatic persistence, actors sleep on inactivity and wake on request/message/alarm, self-hostable or managed; the docs explicitly cite **Microsoft Orleans' virtual actor pattern** as the lineage. ([rivet.dev/actors](https://rivet.dev/actors/), [github.com/rivet-dev/rivet](https://github.com/rivet-dev/rivet), [rivet.dev/agent](https://www.rivet.dev/agent/))
- Orleans itself established the core guarantees you'd want: actors "always exist" logically, are activated on demand, deactivated when idle, and the runtime handles placement — the caller never knows whether the actor was resident.

**Known pitfalls of the shared-pool/state-as-data approach** (from these sources plus multi-tenant OpenClaw write-ups):
1. **Tenant isolation becomes your job.** In a shared runtime, every file write, tool call, and cron job must be tenant-scoped; one plugin writing to a shared path is a cross-tenant data leak. Practical mitigation seen in the wild: root all FS ops at `/workspace/<tenant_id>/` with path-traversal guards. ([KinthAI on OpenClaw multi-tenancy](https://blog.kinthai.ai/openclaw-multi-tenancy-why-vm-per-user-doesnt-scale), [dev.to multi-tenant agent platform](https://dev.to/agentbot/how-we-built-a-multi-tenant-ai-agent-platform-and-open-sourced-it-521g))
2. **Single-writer discipline**: you must guarantee one activation per user at a time (two workers hydrating the same user = state corruption / duplicate replies). DOs/Orleans give you this for free; a DIY pool needs a per-user lock or queue.
3. **Hydration cost**: if the agent's "state" includes a big filesystem (your NanoClaw-like agents have workspaces, installed packages, etc.), loading state on demand is much heavier than loading DB rows. This is the real fork in the road: *agents whose state is conversation + memory files* fit the actor model beautifully; *agents that accumulate arbitrary filesystem/container state* fit suspend/resume (Fly, Modal snapshots) better.
4. **Noisy neighbors** in the shared pool: per-tenant CPU/memory/token quotas are required, not optional. ([KinthAI](https://blog.kinthai.ai/openclaw-multi-tenancy-why-vm-per-user-doesnt-scale))

The KinthAI analysis of exactly your architecture ("one VM/container per OpenClaw user") claims it breaks at **~30–50 users** operationally, costs $500–1,500/mo at 100 users at $5–15/VM, produces a fleet of stale unpatched installs, and estimates ~2 engineer-months to build real multi-tenancy instead. (Uncertainty: this is one vendor's blog with an obvious interest in that conclusion; the qualitative failure modes match other sources, but treat the numbers as illustrative.) ([blog.kinthai.ai](https://blog.kinthai.ai/openclaw-multi-tenancy-why-vm-per-user-doesnt-scale))

---

## 3. Telegram multi-tenant bot architecture

### Bot-per-user vs one bot with routing
- **Hard constraint on bot-per-user:** BotFather allows **20 bots per Telegram account (40 with Premium)**. Programmatic mass-creation of bots is not a supported API operation. A bot-per-user product therefore requires either users creating their own bots and pasting tokens into your signup flow (real friction, but gives each user a truly dedicated bot identity), or it simply doesn't scale on your own accounts. ([core.telegram.org/bots/faq](https://core.telegram.org/bots/faq), [tginfo limits tracker](https://github.com/tginfo/Telegram-Limits/issues/288))
- The common scalable design is **one bot (or a small number), with per-chat routing** to the user's agent: `telegram:dm:<user_id> → agent X`, with tenant context carried via something like AsyncLocalStorage in a Node dispatcher. Multi-bot gateways (many tokens → one dispatcher, identified per-token) are the standard middle ground and are exactly what BYO-token supports. ([mudrava.com bot framework writeup](https://mudrava.com/en/now-every-new-bot-takes-three-minutes-instead-of-a-week/), [hermes-agent multi-tenant routing issues](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/9514), [BOTServer architectures](https://github.com/solyarisoftware/BOTServer/blob/master/wiki/architectures.md), [dev.to design patterns](https://dev.to/madhead/two-design-patterns-for-telegram-bots-59f5))
- If you keep BYO-token bot-per-user: **webhooks let one server host unlimited bot tokens** (route by token in the webhook path). Long-polling per bot means one persistent `getUpdates` loop per token — and Telegram returns **409 Conflict** on concurrent getUpdates for the same token, so polling can't be horizontally scaled per bot. ([grammy.dev/guide/deployment-types](https://grammy.dev/guide/deployment-types), [gramio.dev/updates/webhook](https://gramio.dev/updates/webhook), [BOTServer](https://github.com/solyarisoftware/BOTServer/blob/master/wiki/architectures.md))

### Webhook vs long-polling at scale
- Consensus: polling is fine for dev and single low-traffic bots; **webhooks win at scale** (no wasted requests, lower latency, one endpoint for many bots, works with scale-to-zero since Telegram pushes to you — critically, *polling requires an always-on process, which defeats your scale-to-zero goal*). ([grammy.dev](https://grammy.dev/guide/deployment-types), [gramio.dev](https://gramio.dev/updates/webhook), [hostman tutorial](https://hostman.com/tutorials/difference-between-polling-and-webhook-in-telegram-bots/))

### Idempotency, dedupe, debouncing
- Telegram **retries webhook delivery** if your response is missing or ≥500, and ordering is not guaranteed under retries. Best practice: **ACK the webhook immediately (200) and process async**, dedupe by `update_id` (e.g., Redis SETNX with ~1h TTL), and make handlers idempotent. ([grammy.dev](https://grammy.dev/guide/deployment-types), [gramio.dev](https://gramio.dev/updates/webhook), [core.telegram.org/bots/faq](https://core.telegram.org/bots/faq))
- For agent workloads specifically, **debounce**: users send bursts ("wait", "actually also do X"); queue updates per chat and flush to the agent after a short quiet window (1–3 s) or when the agent becomes free, delivering the batch as one turn. This also gives you the wake-on-message buffer for free: the queue *is* the wake signal. (This paragraph is synthesis from the routing/queueing sources above plus standard practice — no single canonical citation.)
- Outbound rate limits (from Telegram's Bots FAQ): ~1 msg/sec per chat, ~30 msg/sec overall per bot — a shared single bot needs an outbound rate-limiter/queue; bot-per-user mostly sidesteps this. ([core.telegram.org/bots/faq](https://core.telegram.org/bots/faq))

## 4. Capacity math: idle Node.js agent containers per VM

- Container runtime overhead is ~10 MB plus your app's RSS; a general density study puts ~220 MB-average containers at **400–500 practical per 128 GB host** (theoretical 560+). ([OneUptime containers-vs-VMs density deep dive](https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-01-16-containers-vs-vms-density-efficiency-comparison/view))
- Scaling that to your numbers (~150–400 MB RSS per Node agent, no dedup, no swap, leaving ~15–20% headroom for host + page cache):
  - **8 GB VM:** ~15–40 idle agents
  - **16 GB:** ~35–85
  - **32 GB:** ~70–170
  - **64 GB:** ~140–350
  These are arithmetic estimates from the cited per-container figures, not benchmarks — CPU is rarely the binding constraint for *idle* agents; memory is.
- **Density levers, in rough order of payoff:**
  1. **Lazy start / stop-on-idle** (Sablier-style, section 1): the single biggest lever — idle agents cost ~0 RAM; capacity becomes a function of *concurrent active* users (often 1–5% of signups). ([sablierapp.dev](https://sablierapp.dev/))
  2. **zram swap + relaxed overcommit** (`vm.overcommit_memory=1`): compressed in-RAM swap lets you overcommit with "a negligible hit" for rarely-touched pages — idle Node heaps compress well; lz4/zstd tradeoff documented. Commonly cited effective gains of ~1.5–2x on idle-heavy fleets, though exact ratios depend on workload (uncertainty: no rigorous Node-specific benchmark found). ([Debian zramswap manpage](https://manpages.debian.org/testing/zram-tools/zramswap.1.en.html), [zram+overcommit notes](https://copyninja.in/blog/zram_memory_overcommit.html), [systemd-zram-generator guide](https://dev.to/lyraalishaikh/stop-hitting-swap-too-late-practical-zram-on-linux-with-systemd-zram-generator-4m4j))
  3. **Per-container memory limits + `--max-old-space-size`**: Node 20+ is cgroup-aware for max heap, but you should still set the V8 heap below the cgroup limit to get GC pressure instead of OOM-kills. ([Red Hat: Node.js 20+ memory in containers](https://developers.redhat.com/articles/2025/10/10/nodejs-20-memory-management-containers), [IBM article](https://developer.ibm.com/articles/nodejs-memory-management-in-container-environments/), [Node best practices repo](https://github.com/goldbergyoni/nodebestpractices/blob/master/sections/docker/memory-limit.md))
  4. **KSM (kernel same-page merging)**: dedupes identical pages across identical runtimes; 5–10% CPU overhead for scanning. Two caveats: KSM only merges pages marked `MADV_MERGEABLE` (kernels ≥6.4 allow process-wide opt-in via `prctl(PR_SET_MEMORY_MERGE)`; wiring this into containers takes effort), and cross-tenant page dedup is a documented **side-channel risk** — reasonable within one trust domain, questionable across untrusting tenants. ([OneUptime KSM guide](https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-03-04-configure-kernel-samepage-merging-ksm-for-memory-deduplication/view), [Proxmox KSM wiki noting security tradeoffs](https://pve.proxmox.com/wiki/Kernel_Samepage_Merging_(KSM)), [Wikipedia KSM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kernel_same-page_merging))
- Honest caveat: I found no published benchmark of specifically "N idle Node.js agent containers per VM size"; the figures above combine the OneUptime density study with your stated RSS range.

## 5. Provisioning-pipeline hardening for a public free signup

Free compute + public signup is one of the most-abused combinations on the internet, and it's well documented:

- **Documented abuse wave:** crypto-mining gangs systematically farmed free tiers of GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, TravisCI, CircleCI, LayerCI, Render, CodeShip, Sourcehut, Okteto, Azure — cycling new accounts as each free allotment ran out. **TravisCI and Sourcehut killed their free tiers over it**; LayerCI documented the arms race in "Crypto miners are killing free CI." ([The Record](https://therecord.media/crypto-mining-gangs-are-running-amok-on-free-cloud-computing-platforms), [webapp.io/blog/crypto-miners-are-killing-free-ci](https://webapp.io/blog/crypto-miners-are-killing-free-ci), [The New Stack](https://thenewstack.io/how-devops-sites-are-battling-cryptocurrency-miners/))
- **GitLab's countermeasures** (a good template): CI-minute quotas applied to free namespaces, and **credit-card verification for free compute** (card validated, not charged) — the single measure they credit with cutting abuse most. ([about.gitlab.com/blog/prevent-crypto-mining-abuse](https://about.gitlab.com/blog/prevent-crypto-mining-abuse/), [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/2021/05/19/gitlab_crypto/))
- Your agents are *general-purpose compute with network egress on your API bill*, so assume: miners, spam/phishing senders, proxies-for-hire, and LLM-credit farming (people extracting your Anthropic/OpenAI spend for free inference). The LLM-token-farming variant is newer; documented cases are thinner than crypto-mining — flagging that as inference, though the incentive structure is identical.

**Layered checklist synthesized from the guidance:**
1. **Signup friction ladder:** email verification (double opt-in) → block disposable-email domains → CAPTCHA (reCAPTCHA v3 / Turnstile invisible scoring) → phone or OAuth verification for suspicious cohorts → card-on-file only if abuse persists. ([UserCheck free-trial-abuse guide](https://www.usercheck.com/guides/how-to-prevent-free-trial-abuse), [payproglobal](https://payproglobal.com/how-to/prevent-free-trial-abuse/), [suped.com](https://www.suped.com/email-deliverability/answers/how-can-i-prevent-nefarious-email-signups-using-rate-limiting-recaptcha-and-double-opt-in))
2. **Rate limits:** per-IP and per-ASN signup caps; flag multiple signups from one IP range; VPN/proxy detection scoring. ([sensfrx](https://blog.sensfrx.ai/free-trial-abuse/), [UserCheck](https://www.usercheck.com/guides/how-to-prevent-free-trial-abuse))
3. **Runtime quotas per agent (this is where a Telegram-gated product is lucky):** a Telegram account is itself a phone-verified identity — bind one agent per Telegram user ID and much of the fake-signup surface disappears. Then cap per-user: LLM tokens/day, container CPU shares and memory, disk, and **egress** (crypto pools and spam need network; a default-deny or throttled egress policy is the highest-value single control — GitLab/LayerCI both note miners need sustained CPU + specific egress). ([webapp.io](https://webapp.io/blog/crypto-miners-are-killing-free-ci), [about.gitlab.com](https://about.gitlab.com/blog/prevent-crypto-mining-abuse/))
4. **Detection + kill switches:** sustained-high-CPU alerts on "idle" agents (miner signature), per-agent instant suspend (`docker pause`/`stop` is your kill switch), global provisioning freeze flag, and a review queue for anomalous accounts. CircleCI describes running a dedicated abuse-detection function for exactly this. ([The New Stack](https://thenewstack.io/how-devops-sites-are-battling-cryptocurrency-miners/))
5. **Provision lazily:** don't build the container at signup — create the DB record, and materialize the container on first real message. This makes mass-signup attacks cost you ~nothing and doubles as your scale-to-zero onramp. (Synthesis; also the KinthAI onboarding-friction point argues signup-time heavy provisioning hurts conversion anyway — [blog.kinthai.ai](https://blog.kinthai.ai/openclaw-multi-tenancy-why-vm-per-user-doesnt-scale).)

## 6. The "your own isolated server" promise: honesty vs architecture

**Current state of your product vs. the promise:** a Docker container on a shared VM is *not* "a server that belongs only to you" under any technically honest reading — all containers share one kernel, and the 2025–2026 sandboxing literature is blunt that namespace isolation is the *minimum viable* tier: one kernel exploit or mis-mounted socket exposes every tenant. ([emirb.github.io "Your Container Is Not a Sandbox"](https://emirb.github.io/blog/microvm-2026/), [Northflank isolation guide](https://northflank.com/blog/how-to-sandbox-ai-agents), [manveerc sandboxing guide](https://manveerc.substack.com/p/ai-agent-sandboxing-guide))

**How vendors in this exact market phrase isolation — the observable norm is to name the mechanism, not use "belongs to you" language:**
- **E2B:** "each sandbox runs in a Firecracker microVM with a dedicated kernel" — hardware-level isolation, named technology. ([Northflank comparison](https://northflank.com/blog/daytona-vs-e2b-ai-code-execution-sandboxes), [ZenML comparison](https://www.zenml.io/blog/e2b-vs-daytona))
- **Daytona:** honestly positioned as Docker-with-shared-kernel by default, with harder options (Kata/Cloud Hypervisor, Sysbox) for stronger isolation — i.e., it discloses the tier. ([ZenML](https://www.zenml.io/blog/e2b-vs-daytona), [Spheron guide](https://www.spheron.network/blog/ai-agent-code-execution-sandbox-e2b-daytona-firecracker/))
- **KiloClaw** (managed OpenClaw hosting — your product's closest comparable): "each customer runs inside a dedicated Firecracker micro-VM… no shared kernel, filesystem, or process namespace between tenants." ([kilo.ai](https://kilo.ai/openclaw/managed-alternatives))
- Commentary across the space explicitly warns to "separate the marketing from the underlying isolation technology." ([shayon.dev "Let's discuss sandbox isolation"](https://www.shayon.dev/post/2026/52/lets-discuss-sandbox-isolation/), [Northflank "What is a sandbox?"](https://northflank.com/blog/what-is-a-sandbox-and-isolation-technologies))

**Ways to honestly satisfy (or fix) the promise, cheapest first:**
1. **Rewrite the promise** to match reality: "your own isolated agent environment — dedicated container, private filesystem and memory, resource-isolated" is defensible for Docker-per-user; "your own server" is not. Cheapest fix, zero infra work.
2. **Dedicated microVM per user** (Firecracker/Kata/Fly Machines — Fly Machines *are* per-tenant microVMs): lets you truthfully say "dedicated virtual machine with its own kernel," which is how E2B/KiloClaw phrase it. Combined with suspend/stop-on-idle this doesn't have to cost much more than containers. ([fly.io](https://fly.io/docs/reference/suspend-resume/), [emirb](https://emirb.github.io/blog/microvm-2026/))
3. **"Belongs only to you" taken literally** implies dedicated hardware/VM — almost certainly not what a free pilot should promise. Note that if you go the actor-model/shared-pool route from §2, the promise becomes *less* true, not more — you'd need to reword toward "private, isolated agent with its own memory and workspace."
4. Legal-risk note, honestly flagged: I found **no** FTC enforcement action specifically about "dedicated server" isolation claims in agent/sandbox hosting; the marketing-vs-reality risk here is currently reputational/contractual (and generic deceptive-practices exposure) rather than a documented enforcement pattern. ([search corroboration: Northflank/community sources above; absence of FTC cases per search results])

## Synthesis: what the evidence points to for your shape

Two coherent end-states, both well-precedented in 2025–2026:

- **Path A — keep container-per-user, make it lazy** (smallest delta): webhook gateway (always-on, tiny) → per-user message queue with `update_id` dedupe + debounce → supervisor starts the user's container on message, stops after idle; zram + memory limits on the VM; provision on first message, not at signup; Telegram-identity-anchored quotas + egress limits + CPU-anomaly kill switch. Later, swap the backend for Fly Machines (suspend/resume, $0.15/GB/mo idle) to also make the "dedicated VM" claim honest.
- **Path B — actor model** (bigger rewrite, best economics at scale): agent state as DB rows/files (Letta-style) served by a small shared worker pool, or built directly on Durable Objects/Rivet-style actors — zero idle cost, but tenant isolation becomes application-level and the "your own server" promise must be rewritten.

The main genuine uncertainty across sources: real-world resume-latency numbers under load (Fly says "few hundred ms" but no independent benchmarks found), Node-specific zram density gains (no rigorous benchmark), and LLM-credit-farming abuse (incentive-obvious, thinly documented compared to crypto-mining).
